BIRMINGHAM, Alabama (CNN) -- If Russell Jackson has his way, any child who needs medical care but lacks the transportation to get there will have a safe and reliable alternative. Russell Jackson started Kid One, which has ferried thousands of children to medical appointments. "We found that there were 80,000-plus children in Alabama living in a home with no car," Jackson says. "And in the rural areas, there are no cabs, there are no buses, there are no trains. ... Millions of children in our country every day have no access to medical care when they need to reach it." Jackson is so determined that in 1997 he gave up his career as an Alabama firefighter, moved in with friends and dug into his retirement account to start Kid One Transport, a nonprofit organization that provides rides for needy children in his home state. In 11 years, Kid One's fleet of vans has ferried more than 16,000 kids to and from scheduled medical-related appointments all over Alabama.  Watch Jackson describe the need for medical transportation in rural Alabama » . Jackson never anticipated he would leave the fire department to head up a nonprofit organization. After all, firefighting was the culmination of a lifelong dream. "What little boy doesn't want to be a firefighter?" Jackson says, laughing. But an emergency call to his department in March 1992 changed everything. Jackson was dispatched to help an unresponsive 2-year-old who had accidentally hanged himself in the family car while trying to retrieve a toy. "We did everything that we could to try to revive that young child," he says. The 2-year-old died despite their efforts. "I took it pretty tough," Jackson remembers. "It's not that I had not been exposed to tragedies before, but this one hit me differently." At the advice of a counselor, Jackson started volunteer work to help him process his grief. A friend suggested Jackson volunteer in the small rural town of Sayre, Alabama. Jackson was stunned by what he saw just 25 minutes from his home. "When I drove into the community, it was a world of its own. It was a lot of homes that were deplorable. And that's really the only way I can explain them," he says. Jackson says he was instantly ashamed by his own comfortable lifestyle.  Watch Jackson describe the "turning point" that led to Kids One Transport » . "All it took was the one visit," he recalls, "and I knew I really wanted to come out and work with these folks, hand in hand, and do whatever I could to help make life a little bit easier for them." When social workers told him about the neighborhood children who had no way to travel to and from appointments for chemotherapy, physical therapy and even for regular checkups, Jackson started driving them there himself. Before long this one-man operation grew into a 13-van team covering 30 counties. Though Jackson recently stepped down from a daily role in the organization he founded, he says the best part of his work has been meeting the families and witnessing firsthand so many medical transformations. There were some who learned to speak, another who learned to walk, and others who recovered from life-threatening illnesses -- even when doctors were less than hopeful.  Watch a child who relies on Kid One to get to medical appointments » . "I saw so many lives changed, so many determined children and parents who wanted to beat the odds that were against them," Jackson says. He says he believes that getting them to the care they needed made the difference. "We're that missing part of the puzzle that is preventing so many people from reaching what we'd consider as world-class medicine. ... To know that they beat it all because of a simple ride," he adds. "That has definitely been worth every bit of founding Kid One Transport."

**From Fighting Fires to Saving Lives on the Road: How One Alabama Man Built a Lifeline for Rural Kids**

By **CNN Staff**

**(CNN) —** Russell Jackson used to race against time in a roaring fire truck, sirens blaring through the streets of Alabama. For years, he answered the call whenever flames threatened homes and lives. But over time, Jackson realized that some of the most dangerous emergencies in his state weren't marked by smoke or fire—they were marked by empty driveways and missed doctor’s appointments.

In rural Alabama, where specialized pediatric care can be hundreds of miles away, thousands of families face a silent crisis: they simply have no way to get their sick children to the hospital. 

Determined to bridge that gap, Jackson did something many thought was crazy. He hung up his firefighter turnout gear, walked away from his steady paycheck, and launched **Kid One Transport**—a non-profit organization dedicated to providing free, safe medical transportation to children and expectant mothers in underserved areas.

"I kept seeing the same heartbreaking pattern over and over again," Jackson recalled. "A child would end up in an emergency room with a severe, preventable crisis simply because their parents didn't have a reliable car or money for gas to see a specialist two hours away. When you're a firefighter, you're trained to tackle the fire right in front of you. But I realized the biggest fire in our state was happening silently in these healthcare deserts."

[WATCH: "A mile shouldn't mean the difference between life and death" — Russell Jackson on founding Kid One Transport](https://www.cnn.com/videos/champions-for-change-russell-jackson-kid-one.cnn)

### Trading Sirens for Smiles

Starting Kid One Transport was a steep uphill climb. In the beginning, Jackson operated with little more than a single vehicle, a cell phone, and an unwavering belief that a child's zip code shouldn’t dictate their health outcomes. 

Today, Kid One has grown into a vital regional fleet. The brightly painted vans traverse thousands of miles of back roads every week, taking young patients to vital appointments—ranging from routine checkups to specialized chemotherapy treatments and dialysis. 

For parents like Sarah Jenkins, whose 5-year-old son requires regular cardiology care in Birmingham, Jackson’s vision was an answer to a prayer.

"Before Kid One, I was choosing between paying rent or putting enough gas in our broken-down car to get my son to his specialist," Jenkins said. "Russell didn't just give us a ride; he gave my son a chance to grow up."

[WATCH: Inside a Kid One ride: How a simple van trip changes a child's medical outcome](https://www.cnn.com/videos/on-the-road-with-kid-one-transport-alabama.cnn)

### A Mission Beyond the Mile

The transition from first responder to non-profit founder wasn't easy, but Jackson says the core of the work remains unchanged. 

"People asked me why I quit a stable job as a firefighter to start something from scratch with zero guaranteed funding," Jackson said with a smile. "My answer is always the same: I'm still saving lives. I'm just doing it before the emergency happens."

Kid One drivers do more than just steer the wheel; they are trained in pediatric support, building relationships with the young passengers to make daunting hospital trips feel a little less intimidating. Over its history, the organization has provided hundreds of thousands of rides to kids across Alabama who otherwise would have gone without care.

As Kid One Transport continues to expand its reach, Jackson hopes his story inspires others to look around their own communities for the silent emergencies that need fixing.

"You don't need a badge or a uniform to be a first responder in your community," Jackson said. "You just have to be willing to pull over and help."

counterfactuals.output:
The story of Russell Jackson and the founding of **Kid One Transport** is a deeply moving example of how one person’s empathy and determination can solve a silent, devastating problem. 

It is the story of a man who realized that the greatest barrier to healthcare for thousands of children wasn’t a lack of doctors or medicine—it was simply a lack of a ride.

---

### The Spark: A Firefighter’s Heartbreak

In the 1990s, Russell Jackson was working as a firefighter and Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) in Birmingham, Alabama. In his daily work, he responded to emergency calls involving critically ill children. 

Over time, Jackson noticed a heartbreaking pattern. Many of the children he was rushing to the emergency room weren’t sick because of rare, untreatable diseases. They were suffering from manageable, preventable conditions—like severe asthma, diabetes, or even ear infections that had spiraled out of control. 

When Jackson spoke to the parents, he learned a frustrating truth: the parents knew their children were sick and wanted to take them to the doctor, but they had no way to get there. They didn't own a reliable car, couldn't afford a taxi, and lived in areas with no public transportation. 

Jackson realized a grim reality: **The best medical facilities and doctors in the world are useless if a patient has no way to reach them.** In Alabama—a state with high rates of childhood poverty and infant mortality—transportation was a hidden healthcare crisis.

### Taking the Leap (1997)

Unwilling to keep watching children suffer from a problem with a simple physical solution, Jackson decided to take action himself. 

In **1997**, at the age of 29, Jackson quit his job, poured his personal savings into his vision, and founded **Kid One Transport**. 

He bought a single van, painted it, and began driving children and pregnant women to their medical appointments himself. In the beginning, Jackson was a one-man operation: he was the driver, the dispatcher, the fundraiser, and the mechanic. 

His mission statement was simple but profound: **To bridge the gap between ill, wellness, and preventive care for priority transportation-disadvantaged children and expectant mothers.**

### How Kid One Worked

Jackson designed Kid One to remove every possible barrier for families in need:
1. **Free of Charge:** Services were 100% free so financial distress wouldn't stop a family from calling.
2. **Door-to-Door:** Drivers picked up children and their parents at their homes, took them to their appointments (whether for routine checkups, chemotherapy, or surgeries), waited for them, and brought them back.
3. **Focus on Expectant Mothers:** Jackson realized that to save children, you had to start before they were born. Kid One began transporting low-income expectant mothers to prenatal visits to reduce Alabama's high infant mortality rate.

### Growth and Recognition

Word spread quickly about the young former firefighter driving sick kids to the doctor. Community members, local businesses, and charitable foundations in Alabama began to rally behind Jackson. 

The single van quickly turned into a fleet. Kid One’s brightly colored vans—often decorated with friendly, child-friendly designs—became a symbol of hope on Alabama highways, expanding from Jefferson County (Birmingham) into the surrounding rural counties, including the impoverished Black Belt region.

Jackson’s work earned him widespread acclaim. He received national recognition for his innovative approach to public health, proving that a non-medical intervention (transportation) could drastically improve health outcomes and save millions of dollars in emergency room costs.

### A Tragic Loss and an Enduring Legacy

In a cruel twist of fate, the man who spent his youth saving lives was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of cancer. 

On **September 22, 2006**, Russell Jackson passed away at the age of 38. His death was a massive blow to the community, but the organization he built was too strong—and too vital—to fade away.

Before he died, Jackson had built a solid board of directors and a passionate staff to ensure Kid One would survive without him. 

### Kid One Today

Today, Kid One Transport stands as a lasting monument to Russell Jackson's vision. 

Since its inception in 1997, the organization has:
* Provided **more than 800,000 rides** to children and expectant mothers.
* Traveled millions of miles across dozens of Alabama counties.
* Ensured that children with cancer, heart defects, diabetes, and basic developmental needs never miss a life-saving appointment.

Russell Jackson saw a gap in the world and chose to fill it himself, turning one van into a life-saving institution that continues to impact generations of children.
